query: Earlier refractory high-entropy alloys illustrate persistent trade-offs: MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW retained good yield strength from 600 to 1600 °C, with MoNbTaVW reaching 842 MPa at 1000 °C, but both had poor room-temperature fracture toughness and high density; HfNbTaTiZr showed room-temperature ductility above 50% and a yield strength of 929 MPa but only 295 MPa at 1000 °C; and as-cast HfMoTaTiZr achieved about 1600 MPa at room temperature and 855 MPa at elevated temperature but retained a density of 10.21 g cm−3. Given the constraint that density must be reduced without sacrificing the strong room- and high-temperature mechanical performance of as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, what single intervention should be tested? Provide a mechanistic hypothesis, predicted outcomes relative to the as-cast baseline, explicit temperature and loading boundary conditions, supporting evidence from the preceding RHEA results, and a controlled experiment with quantitative rejection criteria that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The substitution of a portion of the heavy refractory elements in as-cast HfMoTaTiZr with lighter elements such as Sc or Y will reduce the alloy's density without significantly compromising its room- and high-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.intervention: Substitution of a portion of Hf and Mo with Sc or Y
generation.conditions: Testing at room temperature and 1000 °C under tensile loading
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary cohesion and lattice distortion
generation.mechanism: The introduction of Sc or Y will reduce the average atomic mass of the alloy, thus decreasing its density. Meanwhile, the smaller atomic radius of Sc or Y compared to Hf or Mo may enhance grain boundary cohesion and reduce lattice distortion, potentially preserving the alloy's mechanical strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: A reduction in density by at least 5% while maintaining a yield strength above 1500 MPa at room temperature and above 800 MPa at 1000 °C, with minimal decrease in fracture toughness.
generation.baseline: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr with a density of 10.21 g cm−3, room-temperature yield strength of about 1600 MPa, and elevated-temperature yield strength of 855 MPa
generation.boundary: Temperature range: room temperature to 1000 °C; Loading condition: uniaxial tensile loading
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of substitution needed to achieve the desired balance between density reduction and mechanical performance preservation is uncertain and requires experimental optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare alloys with varying levels of Sc or Y substitution, measure their density, and conduct tensile tests at room temperature and 1000 °C.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If any alloy variant shows a density reduction of 5% or more without maintaining a yield strength above 1500 MPa at room temperature and above 800 MPa at 1000 °C, the hypothesis is falsified.

Typically, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), comprising a two-phase ordered B2 + BCC microstructure, exhibit extraordinarily high yield strengths, but poor ductility at room temperature, limiting their engineering application. The poor ductility is attributed to the continuous matrix being the ordered B2 phase in these alloys. This paper presents a novel approach to microstructural engineering of RHEAs to form an “inverted” BCC + B2 microstructure with discrete B2 precipitates dispersed within a continuous BCC matrix, resulting in improved room temperature compressive ductility, while maintaining high yield strength at both room and elevated temperature.

Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] .
